about: Evidence sweep for the director's brief, 24 September 2026. 639 places in the project's records where Aaron's words (or suggestions he approved) touch pillars, references, refusals and taste. Every quote was checked against its source by a second reader. authorship=aaron_words means the file attributes the words to him directly; aaron_approved_suggestion means Claude's wording that he approved.

candidate_pillars.pillar: Looks complicated, plays easy. The depth is found by coming back, not studied before you start.
supporting_quotes: "It looks really complicated at first, but once you get going, it's easy to understand." (director-brief-interview.md:19-20, today, asked cold)

"It is an in depth complex game that looks complicated on the surface but you are still able to play the game and learn something new about how things work and interact with next time." (DECISIONS.md:5619)
"I didn't even know about estates until 1000 hours into the game and I had fun still." (DECISIONS.md:5621-5622)
"I want it to be really simple from a user experience level." (docs/design/conquest-ideation.md:953)
"Keep one national pot — for the first real alpha we want this to still be a simple game" (docs/design/economy-ideation.md:289)
"In my mind it should teach you the order of things." (scratchpad/board/decisions/turn-one-teaching-shape.json:3)
candidate_pillars.strength: STRONGEST. He said it on 15 Sep and again today, asked cold, in almost the same words. His rulings enforce it again and again (no troops, one national pot, 'a little too much for now'). The testable form, 'understanding a layer is a REWARD for coming back', is Claude's wording and is listed separately.

candidate_pillars.pillar: Alternate history you can play with: 'what if Texas seceded', driven by the story of the break-up
supporting_quotes: "I was able to simulate what would happen if Texas seceded. And it was a lot of fun to play around with this alternate history." (director-brief-interview.md:20-21)
"the main thing is the story behind the break-apart and how that influences everything." (docs/design/secession-ideation.md:5)
"I like a free texas being fascist because that could be apart of the story that it was taken over by a fascist bloc." (docs/design/politics-ideation.md:2313)

"In the story Texas fell apart, so we will say that because they were going to secede from the union peacefully, Austin is recognised as the actual state of Texas by all other nations" (docs/design/conquest-ideation.md:1378)
"you can kind of experiment and play with different play styles and nations." (director-brief-interview.md:29-30)
"The logic is testing states with the same mission tree but different starting paths" (scratchpad/board/decisions/shared-tree-race-or-checklist.json:3)
candidate_pillars.strength: STRONG. It was his opening thread for round 1 and came back today, asked cold. He repeatedly bends mechanics to serve the story (Austin's legitimacy, Free Texas made fascist, Boston left out). Today's wording ('simulate', 'play around', 'experiment') points to a sandbox, which pulls against the win/lose definition of done (see tensions).

candidate_pillars.pillar: You learn real things about America sideways
supporting_quotes: "Although fictitious it is a history game where I have been able to learn a lot about 15–19th century world history and things about it I would never have learned any other way." (DECISIONS.md:5617-5618)
"I also realized that the state of Jefferson is actually a real thing that people have proposed — I didn't realize that that was actually something that was real." (director-brief-interview.md:22-24)
"I'm ok with allusions as long as they are more historically based. I like this because of the irony." (docs/design/TONE.md:158)
"let's keep Boston separate since they were never the capital of the USA." (docs/design/secession-ideation.md:862)
"their geography and central location, they have the ability to get a lot of money from trade going through them, and they have NORAD and air force bases." (docs/design/secession-ideation.md:1379)
candidate_pillars.strength: STRONG AS INTENT, WEAK IN THE BUILD. He named it first of the three things he loves in EU4 and repeated it cold today. But on 16 Sep he pushed 'any historical context' past the alpha (DECISIONS.md:6038), so as scoped the alpha teaches nothing real.

candidate_pillars.pillar: Ridiculous outcomes, and writing that is funny
supporting_quotes: "The ridiculousness and sometimes hilarious outcomes of the game and writing." (DECISIONS.md:5623)
"My favorite game play has been Provence becoming Jerusalem." (scratchpad/board/decisions/audience.json:3)
"it had a really sharp sardonic voice that was really funny" (director-brief-interview.md:22)
"STATES RISE UP AS WASHINGTON CRUMBLES" (docs/design/TONE.md:292)
"NEW REPORT SHOWS 1 GRAM OF URANIUM CONTAINS 20 MILLION CALORIES" (docs/design/TONE.md:308)
"We told Custer once before and we'll tell him again" (docs/design/TONE.md:180)
candidate_pillars.strength: MEDIUM-STRONG. He said it twice (15 Sep, and cold today), and the headlines and Custer line show the voice in practice. But he deferred 'all jokes and writing like that' past the alpha (DECISIONS.md:6037), and the voice is now bound by rules he did not write ('Deadpan everywhere', 'the game holds no opinion'). Still unresolved.

candidate_pillars.pillar: Everything touches everything: war is one strand of the game, not its point
supporting_quotes: "This isn't a war game. I don't want this to be a game of just war and conquering, where economics and diplomacy help your war effort." (DECISIONS.md:3007-3008; docs/design/conquest-ideation.md:31)
"I want a game where war impacts your economy and your diplomacy and your internal relations, and they all interact." (DECISIONS.md:3008)
"which also means that conquering too much could be a bad thing." (DECISIONS.md:3697)
"An army without finance is no longer an industrial complex." (docs/design/economy-ideation.md:1174)
"people don't like resource extraction in their back yard." (DECISIONS.md:5154)
"poorly treated people makes you look bad to neighbours" (docs/design/economy-ideation.md:1166)
candidate_pillars.strength: STRONG. He set it as the frame for round 2, and the records treat it as binding on every later round. He backed it by drawing 35 arrows on the Sector Wiring page himself. It was not in today's cold answer, so ask whether it is still a headline pillar or has become a design principle.

candidate_pillars.pillar: Every choice has a later price: stringing people along, breaking promises and rushing all come due
supporting_quotes: "tell them to wait — which they will do, but if you never implement it that will make them more angry than if you just declined in the first place." (docs/design/conquest-ideation.md:491)
"With every action there is also an opposite reaction." (DECISIONS.md:4841)
"each of their choices should result in a something that won't be paid off until later on than anything else." (scratchpad/board/decisions/turn-one-teaching-shape.json:3)

"Breaking a peace treaty lessens your relations to all of the nations around you. Let's say that unless you are allied to a country, any country that you border immediately turns hostile. (Because if they are willing to break a peace treaty, might we be next?)" (docs/design/conquest-ideation.md:1950)

"One area per attack, and I want to remove the 3 per turn and cooling down period. If a nation has the money and manpower they can attack and organize as big of an attack as they want." (docs/design/conquest-ideation.md:1726)
"you just got everything done and instead of just starting over from scratch there is a break and you get to see results of actions you took" (DECISIONS.md:5080-5082)
candidate_pillars.strength: MEDIUM. The pattern runs through about a dozen of his rulings, but he has never stated it as a principle. Every slogan for it is Claude's: 'buy now, pay later', 'prices not brakes', 'a player stopped by a rule learns nothing'. Only 'with every action there is also an opposite reaction' is his.

candidate_pillars.pillar: No moral verdict: the game is subjective, and people choose between lesser evils
supporting_quotes: "playing ugly is entirely subjective … the point is that this game is meant to be subjective in that sense." (DECISIONS.md:5889-5890; docs/design/TONE.md:62-63)
"sometimes it is better to be governed by people you don't like rather than worry about being governed by people who hate you" (docs/design/politics-ideation.md:1501)

"unlike current American politics there are going to be coalitions, so they might be somewhat aligned on politics and 100% aligned on separating, but once done there will be more chaos." (docs/design/politics-ideation.md:131-133)
candidate_pillars.strength: MEDIUM. He said it once, firmly, in the tone interview, and it echoes his view of politics as compromise. The wider rule, 'the game holds no opinion; every judgement belongs to someone in the world', is Claude's summary. Today's 'sharp sardonic voice' and his story-driven villains pull against it.

candidate_pillars.pillar: Rooted in the real map: counties, ports, bases, rural against urban
supporting_quotes: "the movement shouldn't be bound to state lines — their goals might reflect state lines, but the movement should be bound to counties." (docs/design/secession-ideation.md:1501-1502)

"as an island nation I could see them being both vulnerable for resources, but also because they have Pearl Harbor, which could be an interesting bonus to their military." (docs/design/secession-ideation.md:1381)
"This is a movement that should only grow in rural areas" (docs/design/secession-ideation.md:1427)
"You aren't dealing with governments, you are dealing with people and communities. No tolls, no nothing." (docs/design/politics-ideation.md:407)
"water may be the best resource in the game" (docs/design/economy-ideation.md:531)
candidate_pillars.strength: MEDIUM. It is how he reasons, almost every time, but he has never named it as a goal. Probably folds into pillar 3 ('learn real things') rather than standing alone.

lookbook.reference: Europa Universalis IV (the game as a whole)
lookbook.what_he_takes: His three reasons, in his words: it teaches real history sideways; it is deep but playable before you understand it, with more to learn each time; and 'the ridiculousness and sometimes hilarious outcomes of the game and writing.' He says explicitly: 'Not so much the mechanics but rather the things I like about it.' Today: 'It is a little bit like Europa Universalis IV, but it's all in a map.'
lookbook.experienced_by_him: YES. Played heavily: over 1000 hours by his own count ('I didn't even know about estates until 1000 hours into the game').

lookbook.reference: His own EU4 run: Provence becoming Jerusalem
lookbook.what_he_takes: A small nation becoming something wildly improbable. He calls it his favourite. GDD §5.0 treats it as the shape of the mission-tree pivots (the United States of Texas).

lookbook.reference: His in-progress EU4 run: the Aztecs beating back the colonists
lookbook.what_he_takes: An underdog reversing history, 'taking the fight to their shore'. A goal that is hard to reach ('tricky').

lookbook.reference: The EU4 world-record run: Oirat becomes the Mongol Empire, converts to Catholicism, becomes Holy Roman Emperor and conquers the world
lookbook.experienced_by_him: NOT his own play; it is someone else's record run. The files do not say whether he watched it. Confirm before it goes in a lookbook limited to things he has experienced.

lookbook.what_he_takes: 'Direction, challenge, story, and bonuses that keep momentum up.' That is Claude's paraphrase (D221), later restated as 'Aaron's four reasons'. This is EU4 machinery taken directly, which pulls against 'not so much the mechanics'.

lookbook.reference: EU4's Holy Roman Empire (the elected emperor)
lookbook.what_he_takes: Federation members periodically elect one member as leader, and that nation runs two budgets. In his words: 'similiar to HRE in EU4'.
lookbook.experienced_by_him: YES, through EU4. He frames it as the EU4 version, not the history.

lookbook.what_he_takes: Its page structure (what it is, how it works, the story behind it, what it touches) as the model for the design wiki. This is process, not creative.
lookbook.experienced_by_him: UNKNOWN. The file only says 'at Aaron's direction'.

lookbook.what_he_takes: A turn model: several things in flight at once. The one-sentence rule ('a turn holds multiple things you can do, none of them finishes in one turn...') is set out as a block quote, but Claude may have worded it.
lookbook.experienced_by_him: NOT RECORDED. No file says he played it. Ask.

lookbook.reference: A hbomberguy YouTube video (he linked it himself; spelled 'hbmomber guy')
lookbook.what_he_takes: 'It needs to talk them through how to play the game like how hbmomber guy talks about it.' He has never said which quality he means (pace, voice, structure, humour). No file describes the video.
lookbook.experienced_by_him: PRESUMABLY, since he supplied the link, but no file records that he watched it or what it is about.

lookbook.what_he_takes: Voice only: newspapers speaking for factions, governing through contested choices, a game that rarely says whether you were right.
lookbook.experienced_by_him: NO. TONE.md states he has not played it. It was the interviewer's suggestion, accepted on a description. It fails the brief's 'only things he has actually experienced' test, so drop it or ask him to play it first.

lookbook.what_he_takes: A federation is many states that remain states, with free trade inside and a flat, automatic 10% internal toll.

lookbook.reference: Texas asking to join the United States (historical)
lookbook.what_he_takes: The movement approaches the nation; the nation does not simply choose. 'similar to when Texas approached the USA back in the day.'
A peace treaty can only be signed with a nation, so signing one amounts to recognition.

lookbook.reference: Distributism and the Mormon law of consecration
lookbook.what_he_takes: The political analogue for Deseret: 'a law of consecration lite… the closest analogue would be Distributist'. Also: 'should be modeled as a distributism christian state.'

lookbook.reference: His own v0.1 prototype, which he played and lost
lookbook.what_he_takes: Failure modes he saw and turned into rulings: territory cut off after a civil war (politics-ideation.md:414), Deseret's own separatists counted as pressure (secession-ideation.md:781), New England eaten early (secession-ideation.md:614).

lookbook.reference: RAND gun-ownership data and Pew Research 2017 figures
lookbook.what_he_takes: Estimates of each county's armed share. These are data, not a creative reference, so keep them out of the lookbook.
lookbook.experienced_by_him: He downloaded the RAND workbook by hand. The Pew citation is his and has not been verified.

refusals.refusal: Not a war game in which economics and diplomacy exist to serve the war
refusals.his_reason: "I want a game where war impacts your economy and your diplomacy and your internal relations, and they all interact."

refusals.refusal: No troops and no troop types
refusals.his_reason: "I want it to be really simple from a user experience level."

refusals.refusal: No rulebook limits on attacking: no three-per-turn cap and no cooldown
refusals.his_reason: "If a nation has the money and manpower they can attack and organize as big of an attack as they want." The limit is resources, not rules.

refusals.refusal: No jokes that touch on racial topics
refusals.his_reason: None recorded beyond "where I would draw the line". His 16 Sep amendment covered only the indigenous half. Claude inferred that the race line 'stays absolute' from his silence (DECISIONS.md:6067), so reconfirm it in his words.

refusals.refusal: No jokes at indigenous nations' expense. This was AMENDED from 'no jokes on indigenous topics' on 15 Sep.
refusals.his_reason: "Missions for the indegenous nations can include dignified allusions and jokes if they are not at their expense." His example: "We told Custer once before and we'll tell him again"
refusals.source: DECISIONS.md:6057-6058; docs/design/TONE.md:180 (aaron_words; supersedes TONE.md:173 in part)

refusals.his_reason: "I wouldn't want to make a joke about death like that."

refusals.refusal: A joke may target the cause, never the suffering
refusals.his_reason: "the joke is at why there is a famine."
"we need to change the whole one action per turn." The later explanation, that a programmer given free rein put it in and nobody chose it, has no quotation marks and may be paraphrase.
NOT RECORDED in his words. The decision is his (conquest ruling 31); the wording and the reason are Claude's.

refusals.refusal: No regional shortages in the first alpha: one national pot
refusals.his_reason: "for the first real alpha we want this to still be a simple game." This refuses scope, not identity.
"Not yet". A deferral, not a refusal.

refusals.refusal: Canada and Mexico are geography, not nations
refusals.his_reason: Not given in his words. It came from Addendum A and was approved.

refusals.refusal: Events may not trigger chains of further events during play; chains belong to the backstory only
refusals.his_reason: NOT HIS. The reason given ('the first thing in this game that runs on rails') is Claude's; he 'took the tighter answer'.

refusals.refusal: Forced expulsion, mass killing and nuclear weapons against cities are never a move
refusals.his_reason: NOT RECORDED as his. This is untagged interview wording in TONE rule 34. Confirm it.

refusals.refusal: No real living politician appears as a leader; a generated leader is a type, never a person
refusals.his_reason: NOT RECORDED as his. Untagged TONE rules 27 and 28. Confirm them.

refusals.refusal: Must not be mistaken for a partisan 'next American civil war' fantasy
refusals.his_reason: NOT RECORDED as his. Untagged TONE rule 41; rule 35 (the partisan player) was proposed to him and accepted.

player: WHO, in his words: "I have created this game for someone who like me and the inspiration draws heavily on EU4. Not so much the mechanics but rather the things I like about it that make it really fun." (DECISIONS.md:5613-5614; scratchpad/board/decisions/audience.json:3)

That person enjoys depth without understanding it: "I went a long time before I understood trade properly and I was still able to play and have fun." (DECISIONS.md:5620). This reversed Claude's drafted audience, 'the grand-strategy player who has bounced off the genre's opacity' (DECISIONS.md:5631).

THE ALPHA TESTER, today: "it was a lot of fun, but honestly, I could see it growing, and it sounds like a lot of the features they've got is going to make it a really fun game where you can kind of experiment and play with different play styles and nations." (director-brief-interview.md:27-30). He judges the alpha on its promise, not on completeness.
PLATFORM, new today and said nowhere before: "it's all in a map, which makes it easier to play on any device." (director-brief-interview.md:24-25). No design document mentions phones or devices.

THE NEWCOMER on turn one is taught: "In my mind it should teach you the order of things." Turn one "would have actions that would walk the player though each of the different systems". (scratchpad/board/decisions/turn-one-teaching-shape.json:3). "It needs to talk them through how to play the game" (scratchpad/board/decisions/turn-one.json:3).

HIS EXAMPLES speak from a nation's seat: "I am Oregon and now I have 26% of my population for the cascadia movement and 26% for the greater idaho movement and that would cause a problem." (docs/design/politics-ideation.md:532)
The player is advised, not rolling dice: "it feels like your generals analysed the data and are giving you a chance to win / succeed." (docs/design/conquest-ideation.md:963)
Between turns the player gets the payoff: "results of trade deals and diplomatic actions you sent out, and new spontaneous things that either make your life easier or harder." (DECISIONS.md:5083)

NOT-FOR, in his words: NONE. Every 'not for' line is Claude's: 'Not the wargamer, not the optimiser... not the player who wants the machine explained to them up front' (docs/design/GDD.md:74), and TONE rule 35, 'not for a player who wants it to confirm that their side of real American politics is right' (docs/design/TONE.md:254, proposed and accepted). The nearest he comes is 'This isn't a war game' (DECISIONS.md:3007).

The project's definition of done, authorship not recorded: 'a playtester who has never seen it can open a link, play sixty turns, and tell you afterwards why they lost.' (CLAUDE.md; quoted at DECISIONS.md:5028). His own answer today never mentions losing.
He playtests himself: the prototype was 'lost by its own designer' (DECISIONS.md:2272). He has sent the playtest link to nobody and will not until the alpha is built (DECISIONS.md:2611, paraphrase).
taste_notes: Real party names over ideological labels, because what a player meets on a ballot is a party. That is his reason, in Claude's words (DECISIONS.md:5516; docs/design/politics-ideation.md:750). He says 'neo-liberal', not 'capitalist' (docs/design/politics-ideation.md:723).
His layout for the political board puts authoritarian at both outer ends, which makes the horseshoe visible (DECISIONS.md:3324, his layout, Claude's description).

He places content by story, not by taxonomy: A Free Texas made fascist 'because that could be apart of the story' (docs/design/politics-ideation.md:2313); Austin as the legitimate Texas (docs/design/conquest-ideation.md:1378); Boston left out 'since they were never the capital of the USA' (docs/design/secession-ideation.md:862).

Headline humour with a double meaning: "STATES RISE UP AS WASHINGTON CRUMBLES" (docs/design/TONE.md:292), glossed as "not like rise up in rebellion but rise up to face the problem." (docs/design/TONE.md:59). Absurd propaganda from a rival paper: "NEW REPORT SHOWS 1 GRAM OF URANIUM CONTAINS 20 MILLION CALORIES" (docs/design/TONE.md:308).

Allusions should be historical, and he likes them for the irony (docs/design/TONE.md:158). Defiant humour spoken by the winning side: "We told Custer once before and we'll tell him again" (docs/design/TONE.md:180).
Names matter to him. On the New Confederacy: "I feel like it would have a different name than just New Confederacy." (docs/design/secession-ideation.md:1442)

He accepts a cruel board: "I think Austin would be wiped out pretty quickly because they have no trade possibility then, but that is ok with me." (docs/design/conquest-ideation.md:1143). On permanent rivalries: "That way it creates impositions and challenges." (docs/design/conquest-ideation.md:1141)
Coalitions of convenience that fall apart after they win: "Movements only work together when they are fighting against the state." (DECISIONS.md:3512); "more chaos afterwards" (DECISIONS.md:3519).
A newborn nation gets a honeymoon: "an extra fervour, like the citizens are willing to overlook certain things." (docs/design/secession-ideation.md:1566)
Pacing across a long game: some movements should grow 'slowly or come in later in the game' (docs/design/secession-ideation.md:1433).
Numbers in human units: food shown as the average kCalories per day a citizen eats (DECISIONS.md:2937).
On the map, occupied ground shows as your territory 'with a different brightness of my map colour' (docs/design/conquest-ideation.md:1011). This is the only visual direction he has ever given.

The newspaper is the form of the game's voice and must ship even with placeholder text: "I still want the newspaper pop up as part of the game." (DECISIONS.md:6038). Local and national news in the alpha; world news later (DECISIONS.md:6024).

He romanticises lawless ground as people rather than governments: "You aren't dealing with governments, you are dealing with people and communities. No tolls, no nothing." (docs/design/politics-ideation.md:407)
He argues from realism: "Mapping this onto a realistic outcome there are two options: conquer, or fails to conquer." (docs/design/conquest-ideation.md:1060)

He thinks in worked examples, not abstractions: tracing milk, petrol, detergent and a pen (DECISIONS.md:2918); a full Houston turn-one script (turn-one-teaching-shape.json:3). "that is me colloquially speaking and we will need to convert this to actual language." (DECISIONS.md:5214)

He answers a choice of options with a third option of his own. Claude records four of its recommendations rejected in round 2 alone (DECISIONS.md:3214, Claude's words). Hostile and Wary are his inventions. Note: he wrote 'weary', and Claude changed it to 'Wary' inside his quotation marks (docs/design/conquest-ideation.md:1182).

His recurring complaint is overload. His own words for it: "A little too much for now." (docs/design/secession-ideation.md:1393). The characterisation 'every complaint... there is too much to think about' is Claude's (docs/design/events-ideation.md:649).
Long commitments: he raised deal lengths himself, from 2/4/8/20 turns to 20/30/40/50/100 turns (DECISIONS.md:5703; the stated reason is not in his words).
Water is his favourite resource ('may be the best resource in the game'), yet he agreed to leave it out of the alpha (docs/design/economy-ideation.md:531, 527).

tensions.a: TODAY, asked cold: "it had a really sharp sardonic voice that was really funny" (director-brief-interview.md:22). 15 Sep: "The ridiculousness and sometimes hilarious outcomes of the game and writing." (DECISIONS.md:5623)
tensions.b: His own deferral: "Lets also push all jokes and writing like that post alpha." (DECISIONS.md:6037). Against rules he did not write: TONE rule 36, 'Deadpan everywhere... no special headline' (docs/design/TONE.md:260, untagged), and Claude's summary 'the game holds no opinion... the game's own voice names mechanics and prints numbers' (DECISIONS.md:5882).
tensions.why_it_matters: The voice is one of the four things he wants a friend to repeat. Right now it is missing from the alpha and hemmed in by deadpan rules that are not his. The brief must say WHO is sardonic (in-world papers, missions, or the game's own panels) and whether an alpha tester meets any of it.

tensions.a: The learning pillar: "I have been able to learn a lot about 15–19th century world history" (DECISIONS.md:5617). Today: "I didn't realize that that was actually something that was real" (director-brief-interview.md:23-24).
tensions.b: "And lets also push any historical context to be incldued post-alpha as well." (DECISIONS.md:6038). TONE.md itself warns that numbers-only panels teach nothing in the alpha (docs/design/TONE.md:456-458).
tensions.why_it_matters: As scoped, the alpha cannot deliver the Jefferson moment he described today. He must say either that the alpha does not test this pillar, or what minimum amount of real-world fact goes in.

tensions.a: "Not so much the mechanics but rather the things I like about it that make it really fun." (DECISIONS.md:5613-5614)
tensions.b: EU4 machinery taken directly: mission trees (DECISIONS.md:4918), the federation leader 'similiar to HRE in EU4' (docs/design/politics-ideation.md:1726), the turn model from Civ2 and EU4 (DECISIONS.md:4740). And today: 'It is a little bit like Europa Universalis IV' (director-brief-interview.md:24).
tensions.why_it_matters: The lookbook has to say exactly what is taken from each reference. If EU4 machinery is in, the brief should own that, or the game risks reading as 'EU4 set in America'.

tensions.a: He loves improbable runs: Provence becoming Jerusalem, the Aztecs taking the fight to the colonists' shore (scratchpad/board/decisions/audience.json:3)
tensions.b: His own brakes on success: "which also means that conquering too much could be a bad thing." (DECISIONS.md:3697), plus the gang-up and coalition machinery. Claude flagged this as unresolved: 'a brake tuned carelessly would flatten exactly the runs that make the best stories' (DECISIONS.md:5646; GDD open question 4).
tensions.why_it_matters: Tuning will settle this by accident unless he settles it on purpose. The brief should say whether the ridiculous run is supposed to be reachable, and how often.

tensions.a: TODAY: "I was able to simulate what would happen if Texas seceded" and "experiment and play with different play styles and nations" (director-brief-interview.md:20-21, 29-30). Economy mode is 'a sandbox with no win condition' (CLAUDE.md).
tensions.b: The project's definition of done: 'tell you afterwards why they lost' (DECISIONS.md:5028, authorship not recorded). The game also has victory conditions and a 200-turn length with victory targets. His Q1 answer never mentions winning or losing.
tensions.why_it_matters: Whether this is a toy you play with or a contest you win changes how aggressive the AI is, how the game ends, and how failure is presented. The definition of done may not be his.

tensions.a: Depth you do not need to understand: estates unknown at 1000 hours, and still fun (DECISIONS.md:5620-5622). Today: 'once you get going, it's easy to understand' (director-brief-interview.md:19-20).

gaps: EMOTIONAL TARGET. He has never said how the game should feel from moment to moment. GDD.md:147 says it is 'absent from the source material', and the three emotions listed there are Claude's.
THE FANTASY / THE PLAYER'S ROLE. Who is the player: a head of state, a government, a party, the nation itself? GDD.md:141 says no such statement exists.
WINNING, LOSING, ENDING. He has never described a good ending or a good loss, or what a tester should feel on reading that they lost. Today's Q1 answer does not mention either.
NON-GAME REFERENCES. He is a filmmaker, yet the records hold no film, TV, book, photograph or painting. The only non-game media is one YouTube video, and he has not said which quality of it he means.
VISUAL IDENTITY. Apart from occupied ground shown as a brighter shade of the owner's colour, nothing on look, palette, typography, period, or what the map should resemble.
PLATFORM AND DEVICE. First raised today ('any device'); never designed or ruled on.
NOT-FOR, in his own words. Every existing 'not for' line was drafted by Claude.
PILLAR PRIORITY. No tie-break rule. Simplicity, story, history and voice have each won in different rulings.

AUTHOR'S INTENT. Why America coming apart, why now, and what he hopes a player understands about the real country at the end. He has not said whether the game has a point of view or is only a sandbox.
SESSION SHAPE. How long a sitting is, where a player stops for the night, and what brings them back. The 'phases of a playthrough' across 50 years are marked 'PARTLY DRAFT' in the GDD.
RIVALS AS CHARACTERS. His turn-one script has Austin 'bragging', but whether AI nations should have personalities has never been ruled on.
DIFFICULTY. How hard the game should be and how forgiving, apart from accepting that Austin could die early.
HUMOUR BOUNDARIES beyond race, real deaths and the indigenous amendment: religion, sexuality, living politicians. The TONE rules on these are untagged and not confirmed as his.
THE TITLE. 'Manifest Disunity': who chose it and what it promises (D217 does not say).
SINGLE PLAYER is assumed everywhere; multiplayer has never been mentioned.
interview_questions: [Resolves tension: the sardonic voice versus deadpan and 'no jokes in alpha'] Your friend said the game had a sharp, sardonic voice. Give me one line from it that made them laugh: a headline, a mission name, something on the end-of-turn screen. Who is saying it, a newspaper inside the world, a rival nation, or the game itself? And does the alpha tester hear any of it?

[Resolves tension: sandbox versus 'tell you why they lost'] It's turn 60 and a tester's nation has just been swallowed by a neighbour. What should they feel reading that: robbed, amused, curious to try again? When they text their friend afterwards, do they talk about losing at all, or about what they tried?

[Resolves tension: improbable runs versus the brakes on big nations] Tell me this game's Provence-becomes-Jerusalem: one ridiculous run, start to finish, the way the player would tell it. Now the neighbours start ganging up on whoever frightens them. At what point in that run should they catch the player, if ever?

[Resolves tension: learning real history versus pushing history out of the alpha] Apart from the State of Jefferson, name two real things a player should walk away knowing about America. Where in the game did they learn each one: a mission, the newspaper, a panel, the map? Does an alpha tester need to learn even one of them?

[Resolves tension: depth you discover versus a turn one that teaches every system] Walk me through a newcomer's first ten minutes: the first thing they see, the first thing they click. Which systems should they not even know exist until turn 30, the way you didn't know about estates?
[Fills gap: who it is not for, in his words] Someone plays for an hour, quits and writes a one-star review. What were they hoping for that this game will never give them?

[Fills gap: lookbook beyond EU4] You're a filmmaker. Name up to five films, shows, books or games you have actually watched, read or played that this game should feel like. For each one, name the single thing you'd steal: not what it's about, but what it does to you.

[Fills gap: emotional target and the player's fantasy] Turn 100, halfway through. Describe the best turn of a player's whole game: what just arrived in the briefing, what they're worried about, what they're about to try. And who are they in that moment: a president, a party, the nation?

[Resolves tension: EU4's feel versus EU4's machinery] Think of the last EU4 session you really enjoyed. What was the moment? Which EU4 systems should this game borrow outright, and which EU4 feelings should it reach by a different road?

[Resolves tension: 'playing ugly is subjective' versus the author's hand] A player crushes a movement with the army and wins. Should the game ever tell them what it thinks of that? Where, if anywhere, should a player feel your own opinion as the author?
[Resolves tension: 'not a war game' versus expansive war rulings] In a good two-hour session, how much of the time is the player at war? What are they doing the rest of the time?

[Resolves tension: how cruel the board may be to a starting nation] A new player picks a nation that is finished by turn 10 because of where it sits. Is that a good story or a bug? What should the nation picker have told them first?

[Resolves tension: 'all in a map, any device' versus pop-ups and screens; fills platform gap] Someone plays on their phone on a train. What's on the screen? When a movement makes demands or the newspaper arrives, does it cover the map or live on it?

[Resolves tension: the indigenous amendment, and reconfirms the race line] Give me one joke the game could make that you'd cut on sight, and one close to the line that you'd keep. Is there any subject, beyond real deaths, where the game never jokes at all?

[Fills gap: tie-break between pillars] When keeping it simple for a newcomer collides with something that makes a better story, which wins? Tell me about a time on this project you chose one, and whether you'd choose the same again.

[Fills gap: author's intent] Why America coming apart, and why now? When a player finishes, is there something you want them to understand about the real country, or is it a world to play in with no message?
[Fills gap: visual identity] Picture the map screen. What does it look like: an atlas, a newsroom wall, a war-room table, a TV election map? Name something real you've seen that it should look like.
[Fills gap: session shape and pacing] How long is one sitting? Where does a player stop for the night, and what pulls them back the next day?
[Fills gap: rivals as characters] On turn one Austin brags to you about being recognised. Should rival nations feel like characters with a personality, or like governments doing arithmetic?
[Settles a ruling: peace treaty versus recognition] Houston signs a peace treaty with the Gulf Compact. Has the Gulf Compact just recognised Houston as a country?
